extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom leaders, media scholars and others interested in funding models for news (subscription vs membership)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative distinctions for choosing and framing news business models — specifically contrasting subscriptions (pay-for-product) with memberships (voluntary support/joining a cause) and their implications for access, mission, and revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscribers vs Members distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: “Subscribers buy a product. Members join the cause.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction as a guiding principle: subscription is a transactional relationship tied to receiving a product; membership is a commitment or identification with a cause. Drawing the distinction opens different ways of supporting journalism and affects decisions about access, engagement, and messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscription = pay-for-product access
rubrics_metrics.description: “When you cannot receive the product unless you pay your share of the costs, that’s subscription.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subscription models tie access to payment (paywalls). This approach works well for outlets that can market a distinctive, high-value product (examples: Wall Street Journal, Financial Times, New York Times). Expect revenue to come from paying users in exchange for exclusive content or services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership = voluntary support and cause-joining
rubrics_metrics.description: “Membership sites typically do not have paywalls… Members join the cause.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership is voluntary and framed as solidarity with the outlet’s mission rather than a purchase. Members may expect the site to remain free for non-members. Membership can be structured as donations and may emphasize participation, civic contribution, and non-monetary support (e.g., donating knowledge or skills).

rubrics_metrics.name: Memberships can be tax-deductible / donation-model
rubrics_metrics.description: Salt Lake Tribune: paid subscriptions (mandatory) will turn into memberships (voluntary, and a tax-deductible donation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider legal/financial framing (donation vs payment). Making contributions tax-deductible changes the relationship and messaging and may support a public-service positioning that prioritizes access over exclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership prioritizes access and public-service goals
rubrics_metrics.description: The Salt Lake Tribune framed membership as expanding access because ‘trusted, independent journalism is a right — not a luxury,’ arguing expanding access is necessary amid misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the organizational goal is to provide trustworthy information broadly (especially in a civic or public-service role), membership models that remove paywalls and prioritize universal access are aligned with that mission. Use membership to justify keeping content free to non-members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mission-driven suitability for membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Membership works well when the publication is organized around a specific cause or civic purpose (example: TPM’s mission to chronicle a national crisis and expose plots against the republic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the outlet has a clear, articulable cause that readers can join; membership is most effective when it can be framed as solidarity with a defined mission rather than only supporting production costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing and transparency with readers
rubrics_metrics.description: “The people at Talking Points Memo are leveling with you.” Membership appeals should be explicit about the crisis/mission and what joining supports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about why the organization seeks members, how funds will be used, and what membership signifies (e.g., solidarity, enabling investigative work). Clear messaging fosters trust and willingness to join the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue composition as an indicator of model reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Talking Points Memo is member-funded in the extreme; 91 percent of its revenue comes from those who have 'joined the cause.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze revenue mix to understand dependence on membership vs ads vs subscriptions. High member-revenue share implies different incentives, sustainability considerations, and expectations from members versus subscribers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different viable strategic choices (subscription-first vs membership-first)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast: New York Times organizes itself around ‘journalism worth paying for’ (subscription-first) vs TPM’s membership-first approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize multiple viable strategies. The subscription-first model emphasizes selling a distinct product; the membership-first model emphasizes mission and solidarity. Choose strategy based on organizational strengths, audience, and values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership as solidarity and civic participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Membership is described as ‘a sign of solidarity’ and may evolve to include donating knowledge and civic skills as common practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design membership benefits and calls-to-action that allow members to express solidarity and contribute beyond money (events, volunteering, expertise). Membership should be presented as participatory civic engagement rather than purely financial support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separating subscription and membership to expand support options
rubrics_metrics.description: “When in doubt, draw a distinction. Subscription and membership are not the same thing. We should separate one from the other. That will open more ways of supporting good journalism.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly distinguish models in strategy discussions and product design to explore hybrid or alternative funding mechanisms; treating them as the same risks missing opportunities (e.g., voluntary giving, nonpaywalled civic access).
